title: Direct Effects of Naphthaleneacetic Acid on Fungi, Bacteria and Microalgae: An Evidence Map with Dose-Response Synthesis and Its Implications for Plant-Associated Microbiology
content: 1-Naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA) is a synthetic auxin used repeatedly in apple production and routinely in plant propagation, yet its direct effects on microorganisms have not been reviewed. We compiled every observation we could locate and verify of a measured NAA effect on a named fungus, bacterium or microalga, drawing on a systematically screened literature corpus, a taxon-directed sweep and targeted database searches, and recorded each with its concentration, replication and evidence tier. The effects were organism-specific. Plant-pathogenic fungi were inhibited at concentrations of 100–400 mg L⁻¹, at which the biocontrol fungus Trichoderma harzianum lost at most 13% of its radial growth. Fungal secondary metabolism was strongly modulated, and inhibition of Saccharomyces cerevisiae occurred in minimal but not in rich medium. Direct bacterial growth inhibition was weak, but the bacterial auxin-catabolism repressor IadR bound NAA with slightly higher affinity than indole-3-acetic acid. Microalgae showed biphasic responses spanning 0.037–18.6 mg L⁻¹. No study measured a microbial community before and after exposure, and no field study measured a beneficial microorganism. We outline implications for biocontrol compatibility, inoculant use in propagation and phyllosphere exposure, and the experiments that would close these gaps.
